headline_marked: Meta adds [[rate limits and $20/month paywall]] to smart glasses' on-device AI features
headline: Meta adds rate limits and $20/month paywall to smart glasses' on-device AI features
summary: Meta's smart glasses will soon limit the "Conversation Focus" feature to 3 hours/month, requiring a $19.99 Meta One Premium subscription for more use, despite the feature running entirely on-device.
details: Meta is introducing "rate limits" and a soft paywall for its smart glasses' Conversation Focus feature. Users will soon be limited to three hours of use per month, with a $19.99 Meta One Premium subscription required for more access. Premium subscribers will get 15 hours monthly.

The company states that a subscription isn't required to use the glasses overall, only for certain AI features. However, the Conversation Focus feature, which amplifies voices in noisy environments, runs entirely on the device's internal chips. It does not utilize Meta's servers or even an internet connection.

This on-device functionality was confirmed by testing, where the feature continued to work even with Wi-Fi, cellular, and Airplane Mode disabled. Meta itself previously described the feature as using "your AI glasses’ open-ear speakers, beamforming technology, and real-time spatial processing."

The move raises questions about the justification for rate-limiting an entirely local feature. Meta has recently faced financial pressures related to AI investments, including layoffs and rebranding some glasses to be cheaper. The company has not yet responded to requests for comment on this decision.

headline_marked: [[Supreme Court to hear Apple's appeal]] in long-running Epic Games antitrust case
headline: Supreme Court to hear Apple's appeal in long-running Epic Games antitrust case
summary: Apple is appealing a contempt ruling regarding App Store fees, after being found in "malicious compliance" for charging developers up to 27% on third-party payments. A ruling is expected by June next year.
details: The US Supreme Court will hear an appeal from Apple in its nearly seven-year-long antitrust battle with Epic Games. The appeal concerns a contempt ruling related to App Store fees, with a decision expected by June next year.

In April 2025, District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers found Apple in contempt of a 2021 order. This order required Apple to allow developers to direct users to third-party payment options for in-app purchases, bypassing Apple's commission.

Epic Games accused Apple of "malicious compliance" for subsequently charging developers up to 27 percent on sales made via these external links. Apple previously took a 30 percent cut before reducing it for many developers in 2020.

An appeals court largely upheld the contempt ruling in December but struck down an order preventing Apple from charging any commissions on external payments. This allows Apple to present new arguments on what it can charge.

The Supreme Court had previously declined appeals from both companies in 2024. However, the justices will now consider Apple's current appeal, though they will not address Apple's argument that the injunction should only apply to Epic.

Epic stated it will "continue to fight against junk fees Apple charges on third-party payments," calling them "illegal and anticompetitive." Apple expressed pleasure that the Supreme Court will hear their case, calling it "an important question of law."
